rationale: A wins because it understands the real story is the risk surface, not the launch confetti. Its best line, "If the company will not disclose the source, do not pitch this angle," is exactly the kind of ugly-but-necessary counsel a founder needs. B has useful bones, but "Novo Nordisk Spent Years Building the GLP-1 Market" drags in names, history, and competitive consequences the update did not supply. That is not seasoning; that is inventing the meal.
gaps_in_A: "Hims & Hers won't say where its compounded semaglutide comes from" overstates the fact. The update says the supply source is not named; it does not prove the company refused to say.

"A newly profitable telehealth company is betting its next chapter on weight-loss drugs" is too grand. The update supports a launch and a profitability milestone, not a company-defining strategic bet.
"already being reported" is not in the supplied facts. The FDA flag and manufacturer pushback are enough; do not add media-context glitter you cannot source.

It leaves the pricing/access fact mostly on the floor. Refusing "Hims & Hers makes weight loss affordable for everyone" is right, but a narrow price-transparency angle could have been salvaged with actual monthly numbers.
gaps_in_B: "Novo Nordisk Spent Years Building the GLP-1 Market" names a specific manufacturer and market history not supplied in the update. The facts say branded manufacturers pushed back; stay there unless you have sourcing.
"entering the space at scale" and "clearest test case yet" are unsupported significance inflation. No scale, patient volume, prescription volume, or market share was provided.
"Hims & Hers Just Hit Profitability. Its First Big Move Carries FDA Risk" invents sequence and importance. Recently profitable plus launching does not equal first big move.
"Ozempic's Price Locked Them Out" presumes patient experience and names a brand the update did not name. The access angle needs real prices and a real patient before it earns that headline.
